questions.q: Why is the absolute magnitude $M$ of a star independent of its distance?
options: It is measured in a filter that removes the inverse-square dilution of the flux
It is defined with the flux at the stellar surface, not at the observer
It is the apparent magnitude corrected for interstellar extinction only
It is defined as the apparent magnitude the star would have at a fixed distance of 10 pc
questions.explain: $M$ is defined through $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\,\mathrm{pc})$ (ignoring extinction), i.e. $M$ is $m$ evaluated at $d=10$ pc. Since $F=L/4\pi d^2$ the flux at a fixed reference distance depends only on the luminosity $L$.
questions.source: Choudhuri 3.2; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: Wien's displacement law $\lambda_{\max}T=\mathrm{const}$ states that
options: hotter blackbodies have their Planck peak at longer wavelengths
hotter blackbodies have their Planck peak at shorter wavelengths
the total emitted power is independent of $T$
questions.explain: Maximising the Planck function $B_\lambda(T)$ gives $\lambda_{\max}T\approx2.9\times10^{-3}$ m K, so the peak moves blue as $T$ rises. The $T^4$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann law for the integrated flux, a different statement.
questions.source: Choudhuri 3.4; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: An optical depth $\tau_\nu=1$ along a ray means
options: the intensity of the incident radiation is attenuated by a factor $e$ (path length equals one mean free path)
the intensity is attenuated by a factor 2
the intensity equals the source function $S_\nu$
questions.explain:
With $\mathrm{d}I_
u/\mathrm{d}	au_
u=-I_
u+S_
u$ the attenuated part of the incident intensity is $I_0e^{-	au_
u}$, so $	au_
u=1$ gives $1/e$. $	au=\int\kappaho\,\mathrm{d}s$ counts mean free paths.
questions.source: Radiative transfer; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: Hydrostatic equilibrium, $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}r=-Gm(r)\rho/r^2$, states that
options: the energy generated equals the luminosity
at every radius the pressure gradient balances the local gravitational pull
questions.explain: A thin shell of density $\rho$ feels gravity $-Gm\rho/r^2$ per unit volume from the mass $m(r)$ inside, which must be cancelled by the pressure difference across the shell. It makes no statement about energy or rotation.

questions.q: The Gamow peak is the energy at which
options: the product of the Maxwell–Boltzmann tail $e^{-E/k_BT}$ and the tunnelling factor $e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$ is maximal
the thermal energy equals the Coulomb barrier height
the nuclei move at the sound speed
questions.explain: Fusion needs nuclei from the thermal tail to tunnel through the Coulomb barrier, with $E_G$ the Gamow energy. The integrand $e^{-E/k_BT-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$ peaks at $E_0=(E_G(k_BT)^2/4)^{1/3}\gg k_BT$ but far below the barrier.

questions.q: What stabilises a white dwarf against gravitational collapse?
options: thermal pressure of the carbon and oxygen nuclei
electron degeneracy pressure resulting from the Pauli principle
ongoing helium fusion in the core
questions.explain: Fermi-gas electrons at density $\rho\sim10^9$ kg m$^{-3}$ have a Fermi pressure $P\propto\rho^{5/3}$ that is independent of temperature and exceeds thermal pressure. This is why a white dwarf can cool without collapsing.

questions.q: The 21 cm line of neutral hydrogen arises from
options: the hyperfine spin-flip of the electron relative to the proton in the $1s$ ground state
questions.explain: The ground state splits into a triplet and a singlet by the magnetic coupling of the electron and proton spins; the transition between them emits at $\nu=1420$ MHz. It is a forbidden line (lifetime $\sim10^7$ yr) but traces cold H I because of the huge column densities.
questions.source: ISM; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: A flat rotation curve $v(r)\approx\mathrm{const}$ at large $r$ implies that the enclosed mass
questions.explain: For circular orbits $v^2=GM(<r)/r$, so $v=\mathrm{const}$ requires $M(<r)=v^2r/G\propto r$, i.e. $\rho\propto r^{-2}$ (isothermal halo). Since the light falls off exponentially this is the dark-matter argument.
questions.source: Galactic dynamics; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: The Eddington luminosity is reached when
options: the nuclear burning rate equals the cooling rate
the Schwarzschild radius equals the photon sphere
the outward radiation force on electrons (Thomson scattering) balances gravity acting on the protons
questions.explain: Radiation force per electron is $\sigma_TF/c$ with $F=L/4\pi r^2$, gravity is $GMm_p/r^2$, giving $L_\mathrm{Edd}=4\pi GMm_pc/\sigma_T$. Both forces scale as $r^{-2}$ so the balance is independent of radius.

questions.q: Hubble's law $v=H_0d$ follows from uniform expansion because
options: galaxies are repelled by the Milky Way
proper distance is $d=a(t)x$ with fixed comoving $x$, so $\dot d=(\dot a/a)\,d=H\,d$
light loses energy to intergalactic dust
it is purely a Doppler effect of peculiar velocities
questions.explain: With scale factor $a(t)$ and comoving coordinate $x$, differentiating $d=a(t)x$ gives $\dot d=H(t)d$ with $H=\dot a/a$. Any observer sees the same law, so there is no centre.
questions.source: Cosmology; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: The CMB was released at $T\approx3000$ K because at that time
options: hydrogen recombined, so photons no longer Thomson-scattered off free electrons
questions.explain: When $k_BT\sim0.3$ eV (not 13.6 eV, because of the huge photon-to-baryon ratio, Saha equation) the ionised fraction collapses and the mean free path grows beyond the horizon. The photons then free-stream and are redshifted by $1+z\approx1100$ to 2.7 K.
questions.source: Early universe; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: For a quasi-static contraction of a self-gravitating ideal gas ($2K+U=0$), the star
options: radiates half of the released gravitational energy and heats up
radiates all the released energy and cools down
stores all the released energy as heat and does not radiate
questions.explain: Virial theorem: $E=K+U=U/2=-K$, so the total energy decreases when it radiates ($L>0$) while $K\propto T$ increases. The release $|\Delta U|$ splits equally between radiation and heating (negative heat capacity).

questions.q: The Jeans mass $M_J\propto T^{3/2}\rho^{-1/2}$ decreases with density because
options: denser gas has stronger self-gravity relative to its pressure gradient, so smaller clumps collapse
denser gas has a larger sound speed
questions.explain: Collapse occurs when the sound-crossing time exceeds the free-fall time $t_\mathrm{ff}\propto\rho^{-1/2}$. A clump of size $\lambda_J=c_s t_\mathrm{ff}$ collapses, with $M_J\sim\rho\lambda_J^3\propto T^{3/2}\rho^{-1/2}$.

questions.q: The distance to a star is doubled. Its apparent magnitude changes by
questions.explain: $F\propto d^{-2}$ gives $F\to F/4$, and $\Delta m=-2.5\log_{10}(F'/F)=2.5\log_{10}4=1.51$. A larger flux ratio means a larger (fainter) magnitude.

questions.q: At fixed temperature the radius of a star is doubled. Its luminosity changes by a factor
questions.explain: $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T_\mathrm{eff}^4$, so $L\propto R^2$ at fixed $T$. Check: $R\to2R$ gives $L\to4L$, which is why giants at similar $T_\mathrm{eff}$ are far brighter than dwarfs.

questions.q: A star's temperature doubles at constant radius. What happens to $\lambda_{\max}$ and $L$?
questions.explain: Wien: $\lambda_{\max}\propto T^{-1}$. Stefan–Boltzmann: $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T^4\propto T^4$, and $2^4=16$.

questions.q: A main-sequence star has twice the Sun's mass. With $L\propto M^{3.5}$, its main-sequence lifetime is about
questions.explain: The fuel supply is $\propto M$ and the burn rate is $L$, so $t_\mathrm{MS}\propto M/L\propto M^{-2.5}$. For $M\to2M$: $2^{-2.5}=0.177\approx1/5.7$.
questions.source: Choudhuri 3.3; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: The core temperature of a pp-chain star rises by 10 %. With $\epsilon_{pp}\propto T^4$ the energy generation rate increases by about
questions.explain: $\epsilon\propto T^{4}$ gives $(1.1)^4=1.46$. The factor 4.6 would correspond to the CNO cycle ($\epsilon\propto T^{16}$) with $1.1^{16}=4.6$.

questions.q: The mass of a non-relativistic white dwarf is doubled. Its radius ($R\propto M^{-1/3}$)
questions.explain: Equating gravitational pressure $\sim GM^2/R^4$ with Fermi pressure $\propto(M/R^3)^{5/3}$ gives $R\propto M^{-1/3}$. More massive white dwarfs are smaller.

questions.q: The temperature of a molecular cloud is doubled at fixed density. The Jeans mass changes by
questions.explain: $M_J\propto T^{3/2}\rho^{-1/2}$, so doubling $T$ gives $2^{3/2}=2.83$. Hotter gas needs more mass to collapse, which is why star formation happens in cold cores.

questions.q: If the dark halo of a galaxy suddenly disappeared, the rotation curve outside the stellar disc would follow
questions.explain: Without the halo $M(<r)$ is the finite visible mass, so $v^2=GM/r$ gives $v\propto r^{-1/2}$. The observed flatness is evidence for $M(<r)\propto r$.

questions.q: The mass of a black hole doubles. Its Eddington luminosity changes by a factor
questions.explain: $L_\mathrm{Edd}=4\pi GMm_pc/\sigma_T\propto M$. A larger mass can hold down radiation pressure from proportionally more luminosity.

questions.q: If the Hubble constant were twice as large, the Hubble time $1/H_0$ would
questions.explain: $t_H=1/H_0$ is inversely proportional to $H_0$. Using $H_0=70$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, $t_H=14$ Gyr, so $2H_0$ gives 7 Gyr.

questions.q: The scale factor doubles during the radiation era. The CMB temperature and the photon number density become
questions.explain: Photons redshift as $T\propto1/a$, and the number density dilutes with volume, $n_\gamma\propto a^{-3}$ (also $n_\gamma\propto T^3$). So $T\to T/2$ and $n_\gamma\to n_\gamma/8$.

questions.q: You use $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\,\mathrm{pc})$ but ignore an extinction of $A=1$ mag. You will
questions.explain: With extinction $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\,\mathrm{pc})+A$. Ignoring $A$ makes the apparent distance modulus 1 mag too large, so $\log_{10}d$ is too large by $A/5=0.2$.

questions.q: The temperature of a radiation-dominated gas is doubled. The radiation pressure $P=aT^4/3$ changes by a factor
questions.explain: Radiation pressure scales as $T^4$ ($a$ is the radiation constant), so $2^4=16$. At fixed density the gas pressure only doubles, which makes radiation pressure dominate in massive hot stars.

questions.q: The solar constant is $S=1361$ W m$^{-2}$ at 1 AU. The solar luminosity is about
questions.explain: $L=4\pi d^2S$ with $d=1.496\times10^{11}$ m gives $3.83\times10^{26}$ W. Forgetting the $4\pi$ gives the too-small $3.0\times10^{25}$ W.

questions.q: With $L=3.83\times10^{26}$ W and $R=6.96\times10^{8}$ m the Sun's effective temperature is about
questions.explain: $T_\mathrm{eff}=(L/4\pi R^2\sigma)^{1/4}=5.77\times10^3$ K. The fourth root makes the result insensitive to modest errors in $L$ or $R$.

questions.q: With $\lambda_{\max}T=2.898\times10^{-3}$ m K, the Sun ($T=5772$ K) peaks at a wavelength of
questions.explain: $\lambda_{\max}=b/T=2.898\times10^{-3}/5772=502$ nm, which lies in the green part of the visible band. Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}=b/T$ means hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths (10 000 K gives 290 nm, in the UV).

questions.q: The Sun burns 10 % of its mass at efficiency $0.007\,Mc^2$. With $L=3.83\times10^{26}$ W its main-sequence lifetime is about
questions.explain: $t=0.1\times0.007\,M_\odot c^2/L=3.3\times10^{17}$ s, about $1.0\times10^{10}$ yr. The 0.7 % is the mass fraction released when four protons fuse to He-4.

questions.q: The Schwarzschild radius $2GM/c^2$ of the Sun is about
questions.explain: $r_s=2GM_\odot/c^2=2.95$ km. The Sun's actual radius is $7\times10^5$ km.

questions.q: The mean density of one solar mass compressed into a sphere of the radius of the Earth ($6.37\times10^6$ m) is about
questions.explain: $\rho=M_\odot/(\tfrac43\pi R^3)=1.8\times10^9$ kg m$^{-3}$, the typical white dwarf density. For comparison, the Earth's mean density is $5.5\times10^3$ kg m$^{-3}$.

questions.q: The Eddington luminosity $L_\mathrm{Edd}=4\pi GMm_pc/\sigma_T$ of a $10^8M_\odot$ black hole is about
questions.explain: $L_\mathrm{Edd}=1.26\times10^{31}\,(M/M_\odot)$ W, so $10^8M_\odot$ gives $1.3\times10^{39}$ W, a few $10^{12}L_\odot$, which is typical of quasars. Radiation pressure on the infalling gas would exceed gravity above this luminosity, so it limits the accretion rate.

questions.q: With $H_0=70$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ the Hubble distance $c/H_0$ is about
questions.explain: $c/H_0=3\times10^5/70$ Mpc $=4286$ Mpc, the scale of the observable universe (about 14 Gpc comoving). It is the distance at which $v=H_0d$ would equal $c$, a convenient yardstick for cosmological distances.

questions.q: The escape velocity from the solar surface, $\sqrt{2GM/R}$, is about
questions.explain: $v_\mathrm{esc}=\sqrt{2GM_\odot/R_\odot}=618$ km s$^{-1}$, a factor $\sqrt2$ above the circular speed at the surface. Compare $v_\mathrm{circ}=\sqrt{GM_\odot/R_\odot}=437$ km s$^{-1}$, so $v_\mathrm{esc}=\sqrt2\,v_\mathrm{circ}$.

questions.q: The Sun orbits at $v=220$ km s$^{-1}$ at $r=8$ kpc. The mass enclosed, $M=v^2r/G$, is about
questions.explain: $M=(2.2\times10^5)^2\cdot8\times3.086\times10^{19}/6.674\times10^{-11}=1.8\times10^{41}$ kg $=9\times10^{10}M_\odot$. This is only the mass inside $r=8$ kpc for a spherical distribution; a flat rotation curve gives $M\propto r$ beyond it (dark matter).

questions.q: Star A has $m_A=3$, star B has $m_B=8$. The flux ratio $F_A/F_B$ is about
questions.explain: $m_B-m_A=-2.5\log_{10}(F_B/F_A)$ gives $F_A/F_B=10^{0.4\cdot5}=10^2$. A factor of 5 magnitudes is exactly 100 in flux.

questions.q: A slab with constant source function $S$ has no incident light, $I(0)=0$. After optical depth $\tau=2$ the emergent intensity is
questions.explain: The formal solution is $I=S(1-e^{-\tau})$ since the background is not attenuated. For $\tau=2$: $1-e^{-2}=0.865$, which tends to $S$ for $\tau\gg1$.
questions.source: Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim) (radiative transfer)

questions.q: The Chandrasekhar mass limit follows from
options: the electrons becoming non-degenerate at high $T$
electron degeneracy becoming relativistic, $P\propto\rho^{4/3}$, so that the adiabatic index is $4/3$ and no stable radius exists
the neutron drip density being reached
questions.explain: For ultra-relativistic electrons $P\propto\rho^{4/3}$ and $GM^2/R^4\propto M^{4/3}/R^4$, so $R$ cancels and only the mass $M_\mathrm{Ch}\approx1.4M_\odot$ can be supported. Above it the star collapses.
questions.source: Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim); Choudhuri 6

questions.q: The CNO cycle dominates over the pp chain in more massive stars because
options: its rate rises much more steeply with temperature ($\epsilon\propto T^{\sim17}$) and the core is hotter
questions.explain: The CNO cycle uses C, N, O as catalysts, so the barrier $Z_1Z_2e^2$ is higher, but the Gamow factor makes it $\propto T^{16-20}$ against $T^4$ for pp. Above $\sim1.3M_\odot$ the hotter core makes CNO dominant.

questions.q: A neutron star is far smaller than a white dwarf of the same mass because
options: the degenerate fermions are about 1840 times heavier, so the same Fermi pressure needs a much smaller radius
fusion continues inside a neutron star
questions.explain: In a degenerate gas $P_F\propto\hbar^2n^{5/3}/m$, so a heavier fermion gives less pressure at equal density and the star must compress until $n$ is higher. The result is $R\sim10$ km instead of $\sim10^4$ km.
questions.source: Choudhuri 6; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: The radius of a Strömgren sphere scales as $R_S\propto(Q/n^2)^{1/3}$. If the gas density $n$ doubles, $R_S$ changes by a factor
questions.explain: Ionising photons $Q$ (per second) are balanced by recombinations $\tfrac43\pi R_S^3n^2\alpha$, so $R_S\propto n^{-2/3}$ at fixed $Q$.

questions.q: Two galaxies have the same radius, but the velocity dispersion of A is three times that of B. With $M\sim\sigma^2R/G$ the mass ratio $M_A/M_B$ is
questions.explain: The virial theorem gives $M\propto\sigma^2R$, so for equal $R$, $M_A/M_B=3^2=9$. Equivalently $M\sim\sigma^2R/G$, which is how dynamical masses of clusters are estimated.

questions.q: Superluminal motion ($v_\mathrm{app}>c$) of jet blobs is explained by
options: gravitational lensing by the host galaxy
a projection effect of a relativistic jet pointing close to the line of sight
questions.explain: For $v\approx c$ at angle $\theta$ to the line of sight, $v_\mathrm{app}=v\sin\theta/(1-(v/c)\cos\theta)$ can exceed $c$ because the blob nearly catches up with its own light. Nothing travels faster than $c$.
questions.source: Active galaxies; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: The H$\alpha$ line (rest $656.3$ nm) of a galaxy is observed at $984.5$ nm. What are $z$ and $a(t_\mathrm{emit})/a(t_0)$?
questions.explain: $1+z=\lambda_\mathrm{obs}/\lambda_\mathrm{em}=a(t_0)/a(t_\mathrm{em})=1.5$, so $z=0.5$ and $a(t_\mathrm{em})/a(t_0)=1/1.5=0.67$. Always compute $1+z$ first; the scale factor at emission is then simply its inverse.

questions.q: After matter–radiation equality, the ratio $\rho_r/\rho_m$ scales with the scale factor as
questions.explain: $\rho_r\propto a^{-4}$ (photon number dilutes and each photon redshifts) and $\rho_m\propto a^{-3}$, so the ratio decreases as $a^{-1}$ and matter dominates. Equality is at $z\approx3400$; afterwards $\rho_r/\rho_m\propto1/a$ keeps falling.
questions.source: Early universe; Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim)

questions.q: A star has the same $T_\mathrm{eff}$ as the Sun but 100 times its luminosity. Its radius is about
questions.explain: $L\propto R^2T^4$, so at equal $T$, $R/R_\odot=\sqrt{L/L_\odot}=10$. Stefan-Boltzmann: $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T_\mathrm{eff}^4$, so a factor 100 in $L$ at fixed $T$ means a factor 10 in $R$.
questions.source: Refregier MC style (adapted, not verbatim) (HR diagram)

questions.q: When a Sun-like star exhausts hydrogen in its core and becomes a red giant, then
options: the core expands and cools while the envelope contracts
the inert He core contracts and heats while the envelope expands and cools
the whole star contracts and heats
hydrogen burning stops everywhere and the luminosity drops
questions.explain: H-shell burning above the inert He core deposits ash on it, so the core contracts (virial theorem, heats) while the envelope expands to large $R$ at low $T_\mathrm{eff}$. The luminosity increases.

questions.q: Proxima Centauri has a parallax of 768 milliarcseconds. How far away is it?
questions.explain: $d[\mathrm{pc}]=1/p[\mathrm{arcsec}]=1/0.768=1.30$ pc. Quick check: $1/0.75=4/3$. The parallax is the angle subtended by 1 AU, so a parallax of 1 arcsec means 1 pc.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2025_Winter_Session MC 2, not verbatim

questions.q: Two main-sequence stars differ in mass by a factor of 3. Approximately how much longer does the lower-mass star live?
questions.explain: Lifetime = fuel/luminosity $\propto M/L$ and $L\propto M^3$, so $\tau\propto M^{-2}$ and $\tau_{\rm low}/\tau_{\rm high}=3^2=9$ (with $L\propto M^{3.5}$ one would get $3^{2.5}\approx15$; the course uses $M^{-2}$).
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2025_Winter_Session MC 5, not verbatim

questions.q: Relativistic electrons with an energy distribution $N(E)\propto E^{-3}$ radiate synchrotron emission in a magnetic field. The spectrum $f(\nu)$ is
questions.explain:
For $N(E)\propto E^{-p}$ the synchrotron spectrum is $f(
u)\propto
u^{(1-p)/2}$ (each electron radiates mainly at $
u\propto E^2B$). With $p=3$: $
u^{-1}$; the exam's $p=2$ gives $
u^{-1/2}$.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2025_Winter_Session MC 11, not verbatim

questions.q: A galaxy has the redshift $z=0.05$. For $H_0=70$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and Hubble's law, its distance is about
questions.explain: For $z\ll1$, $v\approx cz=1.5\times10^4$ km/s and $d=v/H_0=1.5\times10^4/70\approx214$ Mpc. Estimate: $3\times10^5\times0.05/70\approx200$.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2025_Winter_Session MC 13, not verbatim

questions.q: The 21 cm line (rest frequency 1420 MHz) of a distant galaxy is observed at 473 MHz. At which redshift was it emitted?
questions.explain: $1+z=\nu_{\rm em}/\nu_{\rm obs}=1420/473=3.0$, so $z=2$. Frequencies and wavelengths scale oppositely: $1+z=\lambda_{\rm obs}/\lambda_{\rm em}=63$ cm/21 cm.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2025_Winter_Session MC 14, not verbatim

questions.q: The 'curve of growth' describes the relation between
options: the equivalent width of a spectral line and the column density of the absorbing gas
the amplitude of density perturbations and time
the Einstein coefficients and the energy difference of a two-level system
the luminosity of an AGN and the mass of its black hole
questions.explain: Equivalent width $W$ against column density $N$: linear for weak (optically thin) lines, flat (saturated) when the line core is optically thick, and rising again $\propto\sqrt N$ when the damping wings take over. It is the tool to get abundances from absorption lines.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2024_Winter_Session MC 9, not verbatim

questions.q: Solar neutrino detectors that are sensitive only to electron neutrinos $\nu_e$ find roughly
options: one third of the $\nu_e$ flux predicted by solar models
the predicted flux, but only $\nu_\mu$ and $\nu_\tau$
questions.explain: The Sun emits only $\nu_e$ (pp chain, $^8$B), but flavour oscillation (neutrinos have mass) converts them on the way, so on average one third arrive as $\nu_e$; the total flux of all flavours agrees with the model (SNO). This was the 'solar neutrino problem'.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2024_Winter_Session MC 6, not verbatim

questions.q: The ionised intracluster medium of a galaxy cluster has the same temperature and metallicity everywhere. In a region where the gas density is twice as large, the thermal bremsstrahlung emissivity (X-rays) is
questions.explain: Emissivity $\propto n_en_p\propto\rho_{\rm gas}^2$ (collisions between electrons and ions), so $2^2=4$. This is why the X-ray image is concentrated on the dense cluster centre and why $\rho_{\rm gas}$ can be deprojected from it.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2024_Winter_Session MC 12, not verbatim

questions.q: A massive object moves through a collisionless sea of lighter stars. Dynamical friction is a net gravitational force on the object
options: backwards, because the stars it has attracted pile up in its wake
forwards, because the stars it has attracted pile up in its wake
backwards, because the density in its wake is reduced
forwards, because the density in its wake is reduced
questions.explain: The object pulls stars towards its path, creating an over-density behind it; that over-density pulls it back (Chandrasekhar: $\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}t\propto-G^2M\rho/v^2$). It slows massive satellites, globular clusters and black holes, which sink to the centre.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2024_Summer_Session MC 9, not verbatim

questions.q: In the Jeans analysis of a non-expanding fluid, a perturbation with wavelength $\lambda<\lambda_J$ will
questions.explain: Dispersion relation $\omega^2=c_s^2k^2-4\pi G\rho_0$. For $k>k_J$ (i.e. $\lambda<\lambda_J$) $\omega^2>0$: pressure wins, the mode is an oscillating sound wave; for $k<k_J$ $\omega^2<0$ and the mode grows (collapse). $M_J\propto\lambda_J^3$.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2024_Summer_Session MC 10, not verbatim

questions.q: Cloud 1 has uniform density $\rho_0$ and diameter $D$. Cloud 2 has the same composition and constant opacity, uniform density $4\rho_0$ and diameter $D/2$. Along a line of sight through the centres, the optical depths compare as
questions.explain: $\tau=\int\chi\rho\,\mathrm ds=\chi\rho L$: $\tau_1=\chi\rho_0D$ and $\tau_2=\chi\,4\rho_0\,D/2=2\chi\rho_0D=2\tau_1$. (In the exam the density ratio is 2, which gives equal optical depths.)
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2024_Summer_Session MC 3, not verbatim

questions.q: The Sun is about 8 kpc from the Galactic Centre. A star is 6 kpc from us in the direction of Galactic longitude $l=180^\circ$, latitude $b=0^\circ$. Its distance from the Galactic Centre is about
questions.explain: $l=180^\circ$ points directly away from the Galactic Centre (which is at $l=0^\circ$), so the distances add: $8+6=14$ kpc. For $l=0^\circ$ it would be $|8-6|=2$ kpc.
questions.source: adapted from Astro_I_2024_Summer_Session MC 2, not verbatim
